items.prompt: What is simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)?
items.answer: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

questions.question: What is the role of virtual reality software in producing a virtual reality experience?
options: To replace VR or AR hardware by generating output data directly
To convert high-level developer descriptions into device drivers only
To track the surrounding physical environment instead of the user
To drive VR or AR hardware so it generates appropriate stimuli for human sense organs
questions.explanation: VR software drives VR or AR hardware so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a VR experience.

data.text: VR software drives virtual reality or augmented reality hardware to generate appropriate stimuli. These stimuli are received by human sense organs to create a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.
points: VR software drives hardware to generate stimuli that stimulate human senses.

questions.question: In a VR system, which pair of processes occurs between the user and the VR hardware?
options: Interaction and rendering
Environment modeling and object modeling
Tracking and stimulation
Input queuing and output synchronization
questions.explanation: The VR data-flow description states that tracking and stimulation occur between the user and the VR hardware.

questions.question: How does data move between a user and a VR hardware system?
options: The physical world generates data, the system processes it, and the hardware generates stimuli for the sense organs.
Input devices generate stimuli, the system processes them, and output devices generate data for the sense organs.
Output devices generate data, the system processes it, and input devices generate stimuli for the sense organs.
Input devices generate data, the system processes it, and output devices generate stimuli for the sense organs.
questions.explanation: The user operates input devices to generate data that is processed by the VR system, and the processed data is sent back to output devices that generate stimuli for the sense organs.

questions.question: What design and software support is required for the data flow between a user and VR hardware?
options: Interaction design, rendering, and software that processes input and generates output.
Interaction design, perceptual design, and software that processes input and generates output.
Interaction design, perceptual design, and software that tracks the head.
Environment modeling, perceptual design, and software that processes input and generates output.
questions.explanation: The data flow requires interaction design and modeling for input devices, perceptual design and modeling for output stimuli, and software to process input data and generate output data.

questions.question: Which two components represent the software part of the VR data-flow diagram?
options: The virtual world generator and a middleware component
The software-and-database component and a renderer component
The VR engine and a head-tracker component
The VR engine and a software-and-database component
questions.explanation: The software part of the VR data-flow diagram is represented by the VR engine and a software-and-database component.

data.text: Virtual reality systems involve bidirectional data flows between the hardware, the physical world, and the user. This data flow works by processing user input data to generate output data that suitably affects the user's sense organs. These flows require proper interaction design for inputs, perceptual design for stimuli, and software for processing. The software part specifically includes a virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.
points: Virtual reality systems involve bidirectional data flows between the hardware, the physical world, and the user.
The data flow works by processing user input data to generate output data that suitably affects the user's sense organs.
Data flow requires proper interaction design for inputs, perceptual design for stimuli, and software for processing.
The software components include a virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

steps: User operates input devices to generate data
Data is sent to the virtual reality system for processing

questions.question: Which three activities are involved in creating a VR experience?
options: Generating visual output, aural output, and haptic output
Queuing input events, maintaining virtual reality, and synchronizing displays
Creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions
Capturing a physical world, applying SLAM, and mapping textures
questions.explanation: Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering the stereoscopic view, and incorporating interactions that use tracking hardware.

questions.question: In VR experience creation, what do the terms view or rendering broadly refer to?
options: Only stereoscopic visual output
Output for the visual sense and other senses
Only input from tracking hardware
Only the modeled virtual environment
questions.explanation: View or rendering is used broadly to include not only visual output but also output for other senses.

questions.question: What kind of support ideally should VR software provide to a developer?
options: High-level descriptions generate low-level details, while middleware or original from-scratch functions can also be used
Developers must directly implement device drivers, head tracking, and display output
Low-level instructions generate high-level details, and developers must write all middleware
Developers can only call middleware functions and cannot design original functions
questions.explanation: Ideally, VR software lets developers provide high-level descriptions from which low-level details are determined, using middleware and libraries or designing functions from scratch.

questions.question: In practical VR development, what role can an SDK for a particular headset or platform play?
options: It automatically turns every high-level description into low-level VR details
It is platform independent across different hardware and operating systems
It handles lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output
It lets the developer avoid understanding any platform-specific operations
questions.explanation: A practical VR developer may use a platform-dependent SDK to handle lowest-level platform-specific operations, while still needing to understand that SDK.

questions.question: What is a practical trade-off of using a game engine as middleware for VR development?
options: It guarantees full flexibility for ideas not part of standard video games
It must be a VR-specific engine before it can be used as middleware
It can reduce initial effort but may limit flexibility for ideas outside standard video games
It removes the need for any platform SDK or lowest-level operations
questions.explanation: A game engine can be adopted as VR middleware and save initial effort, but if it is not VR-specific it can be cumbersome and less flexible for non-standard VR ideas.

data.text: Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering, and incorporating interactions. While ideal software would let developers provide high-level descriptions, practical development often requires implementing functionality from scratch or using platform-specific SDKs. Game engines can be used as middleware, but they may be cumbersome and less flexible for ideas that fall outside of standard video games.
points: Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering, and incorporating interactions.
Ideal VR software would allow developers to provide high-level descriptions while still allowing for original work from scratch.
In practice, developers may need to implement much functionality from scratch using platform-specific SDKs.
Game engines can be used as middleware, but they may be cumbersome and less flexible for non-standard ideas.

questions.question: In the virtual reality software model, what is the virtual world generator treated as?
options: A black-box abstraction of the entire VR software system
An internal model of every hardware driver
A renderer that sends data to one display
A queue that orders simultaneous input events
questions.explanation: The virtual world generator is an abstraction of the whole VR software system and is treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.

questions.question: In a virtual world generator, why are simultaneous input events from a head tracker, keyboard, mouse, or game controller placed in a queue?
options: So they can be processed systematically
To synchronize output devices with input data
To convert input events into renderer output
To make the internal reality appear real
questions.explanation: Simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

questions.question: Which set lists output renderers that a virtual world generator can use?
options: Visual, aural, and haptic renderers
Input queue, internal reality, and display output
Head tracker, keyboard, and game controller
SLAM, texture mapping, and mesh generation
questions.explanation: The virtual world generator can use several output renderers, including visual, aural, and haptic renderers.

questions.question: In creating a virtual world, what does texture mapping do?
options: Captures the real world using SLAM techniques
Maps camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object
Keeps output devices synchronized with incoming input data
Defines a triangular mesh in three-dimensional space
questions.explanation: Texture mapping is a way of creating a virtual world by mapping camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object.

questions.question: What must be defined and maintained for a completely synthetic virtual world?
options: Camera capture, computer vision, and SLAM techniques
A triangular mesh and material/physical surface properties
An aural renderer, haptic renderer, and input queue
A head tracker, keyboard, and game controller
questions.explanation: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in 3D and maintaining material and physical surface properties.

data.text: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the virtual reality software system that receives and systematically processes inputs from various devices. It maintains an internal reality and synchronizes these inputs with visual, aural, and haptic renderers. Additionally, VR software supports the creation of synthetic worlds through computer-graphics operations and recorded physical worlds using computer vision and SLAM techniques.
points: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the virtual reality software system.
The VWG receives inputs from various devices and processes them systematically in a queue.
The VWG maintains an internal reality and synchronizes inputs with visual, aural, and haptic renderers.
VR software supports synthetic worlds through computer-graphics operations and recorded physical worlds using computer vision and SLAM techniques.

questions.question: What is matched motion in virtual reality?
options: A menu operation that sends a user to a selected virtual location
A place where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align
Moving oneself in the virtual world while real physical motion is not matched
Maintaining correspondence between a user's real-world motions and virtual-world motions
questions.explanation: Matched motion is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.

questions.question: What is a matched zone in VR?
options: A virtual obstacle without a corresponding physical obstacle
A safe real-world region with restricted physical movement where real and virtual worlds align
A selected virtual location reached without physical movement
A visual viewpoint chosen by the renderer for a head motion
questions.explanation: A matched zone is a place where the real world and virtual world perfectly align, corresponding to the safe real-world region where physical movement is restricted.

questions.question: Which situation describes an obstacle mismatch in an immersive VR application?
options: A user remains seated while their avatar walks through the virtual world
A virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone
A user's physical movement is translated to another part of the virtual world
A physical obstacle in the matched zone has a corresponding virtual obstacle
questions.explanation: An obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle lacks a corresponding virtual obstacle.

questions.question: What is user locomotion in VR?
options: Maintaining correspondence between real-world and virtual-world motions
Moving oneself in the virtual world while the real-world physical motion is not matched
Translating movement within a safe region to movement elsewhere in the virtual world
Pointing to a desired virtual location and being sent there without physical movement
questions.explanation: User locomotion is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched.

questions.question: Why should VR software include support for different sorts of user locomotion?
options: So that virtual obstacles always correspond to physical obstacles in the matched zone
So that matched motion can be maintained for every body part
So that cyber sickness can be addressed
So that the visual renderer can always use the correct head viewpoint
questions.explanation: Locomotion operations that avoid physical movement may lead to cyber sickness, and support for different locomotion sorts should be part of VR software so that cyber sickness can be addressed.

data.text: Matched motion maintains correspondence between real-world and virtual motions. A matched zone is an area where physical movements are translated into virtual motions, and VR software helps developers manage these correspondences. User locomotion allows movement in the virtual world without matching physical movement, with VR software providing options like teleportation or vehicle metaphors to address cybersickness.
points: Matched motion maintains correspondence between real-world and virtual motions.
A matched zone is an area where physical movements are translated into virtual motions.
VR software helps developers manage matched-motion challenges and correspondences.
User locomotion is moving in the virtual world without matching physical movement.
VR software supports locomotion methods like teleportation and vehicle metaphors to address cybersickness.

questions.question: How does virtual reality software turn the bidirectional data flow between a user and hardware into a controlled virtual reality experience?
questions.reference_answer: In a virtual reality system, data flows bidirectionally between the hardware, the physical world, and the user, with tracking and stimulation occurring between the user and the hardware. The user operates input devices to generate data for the system, and the system sends processed data back to output devices that generate stimuli affecting the user's sense organs. Proper interaction and perceptual design and modeling, plus software, ensure the data flow drives the hardware so the stimuli suitably stimulate the human sense organs and create a virtual reality experience.

questions.question: How does the virtual world generator coordinate a virtual reality system's inputs, internal world, and multiple sensory outputs?
questions.reference_answer: The virtual world generator is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality software, treated as a black box. It receives low-level input from devices such as a head tracker, keyboard, mouse, and game controller, and queues simultaneous input events. It maintains an internal reality, converts incoming input into renderer output, and keeps output synchronized with input to maintain an input-output match. It can drive visual, aural, and haptic renderers for different displays.

questions.question: How do matched motion and user locomotion differ in virtual reality, and why can teleportation be a useful locomotion choice?
questions.reference_answer: Matched motion maintains correspondence between a user's real-world motions and the virtual world, with a matched zone where real and virtual worlds align and physical movement is restricted. User locomotion moves the user through the virtual world while the user's real motion is not matched, often to move outside the matched zone. Some locomotion operations that avoid physical movement may lead to cybersickness, but teleportation sends the user to a selected virtual location without physical movement and, as an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement. Software should support different locomotion operations so cybersickness can be addressed.

questions.question: Why might a virtual reality developer use a headset software development kit together with a game engine as middleware, and what limitation does a non-virtual-reality game engine have?
questions.reference_answer: Virtual reality software should help a developer create a virtual environment, render the stereoscopic output view, and incorporate interaction, ideally from high-level descriptions that determine low-level details automatically. A platform-dependent software development kit can handle lowest-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output, while a game engine can act as middleware to avoid substantial initial effort. In practice the developer may still implement functionality from scratch, and if the game engine is not specifically a virtual reality engine it can be cumbersome for ideas outside standard video games and reduce flexibility.
